name: Source bias
statement: Attaching an identical message to a trusted or a distrusted source changes how far it moves opinion, and in the founding study it changed nothing about how much of the message people learned.
meaning: Source bias is a label rather than a finding, and at least three literatures answer to it. The first is source credibility in persuasion: the same argument shifts opinion further when a trusted communicator is named. The second is the sleeper effect, a delayed rise in agreement with a message that was discounted when it was heard. The third is the partisan source cue, where people move towards the position their own party's leaders take. Two neighbouring entries in this atlas cover adjacent ground, authority bias for compliance with an instruction and the hostile media effect for partisan readings of one report. This entry keeps the first claim, which has the longest measured record, and reports the other two where they bear on it. The claim is narrower than the name suggests. Trust in the source changed what Hovland and Weiss's readers accepted, and it did not change what they learned.

origin.who: Carl I. Hovland and Walter Weiss
origin.note: The paper is titled 'The Influence of Source Credibility on Communication Effectiveness' and it does not use the phrase source bias. Its second question, whether opinion change from a distrusted source grows over time, was inherited from Hovland, Lumsdaine and Sheffield's 1949 book, which had named the sleeper effect using a single source.

evidence:
Hovland and Weiss ran an advanced undergraduate history class at Yale. Each student read a booklet of four articles, on antihistamine drugs, atomic submarines, the steel shortage and the future of cinema, with the author or publication named at the end of each. Two sources in every booklet had been picked as high credibility and two as low. A pre-test five days earlier had confirmed the split: 94.7% of raters called the New England Journal of Biology and Medicine trustworthy and 5.9% said the same of a mass-circulation pictorial magazine, 93.7% for Robert J. Oppenheimer against 1.3% for Pravda, 80.9% for the Bulletin of National Resources Planning Board against 17.0% for a syndicated right-wing columnist, and 89.2% for Fortune against 21.2% for a film-gossip columnist. Opinion was measured before, immediately after and four weeks after. Data came from 223 subjects in total, and the main analysis rests on the 61 students present at all three sessions, giving 244 communications and 122 per credibility group.

Net opinion change in the direction advocated was 23.0% for high-credibility sources and 6.6% for low, a gap of 16.4 percentage points, p < .01. Rerunning the analysis on each student's own trustworthiness rating gave 22.5% against 8.4%, a gap of 14.1 points, p < .03. Factual learning did not follow. On the four-item quizzes, readers of high-credibility sources averaged 3.36 items correct against 3.26 for low, p = .35, and after four weeks 2.58 against 2.67, p = .46.

Judgements of the articles moved with the name attached. Among readers who already agreed with the position, 78.3% called the high-credibility author fair against 60.5% for the low-credibility author. In 14 of 16 comparisons the low-credibility source was rated less fair or less justified, on articles that were word for word identical.

Between the immediate test and the four-week test the two curves crossed. Agreement fell by 10.7 percentage points for the high-credibility sources and rose by 7.4 for the low, a difference of 18.1 points, p = .001. Recall of who had written each article ran between 85.7% and 93.4% immediately and between 55.3% and 76.7% at four weeks. The lowest of those four figures came from readers who had disagreed with an untrustworthy source, the group in which the sleeper pattern appears.

replication.headline: A distrusted source reliably dampens persuasion by a message, and reliably fails to dampen belief in a news headline. The sleeper effect that arrived with the finding is the weaker half: pooled across 72 data sets, delayed change after a discounting cue is d = 0.08, the same figure as in readers given no message at all.
replication.detail:
Kumkale and Albarracín searched to March 2003 and found 24 eligible reports holding 72 data sets. Change from the immediate to the delayed test in discounting-cue conditions came to d+ = 0.08, fixed-effects 95% CI 0.03 to 0.13, k = 72, N = 2,480. Acceptance-cue conditions decayed over the same interval, d+ = -0.21, CI -0.27 to -0.15, k = 47, N = 1,589, and the difference between the two was reliable, B = -0.29, SE = 0.04, QB(1) = 58.15, p < .0001. The 0.08 is what makes the verdict awkward for the textbook version, because no-message control conditions also changed by 0.08, CI -0.02 to 0.20, k = 13. Rise relative to a credible source is there; rise above doing nothing is not. The pattern held only in a corner of the literature: where recipients were motivated and able to think and met the discounting cue after the arguments, the average change was 0.25, p < .01. Sleeper effects were larger where initial change was closest to zero, B = -0.48, SE = 0.16, p < .01, k = 26, which is to say the cue has to work before it can wear off.

On the persuasion side the modern record is uneven rather than empty. Clemm von Hohenberg and Guess built a fictitious news outlet so that credibility could be manipulated rather than assumed. Their abstract reports that the treatments raised trust in the outlet for up to ten days. It also reports some evidence of stronger persuasion on more partisan topics, and none on a less politicised issue, a result the authors call mixed.

On judgements of truth the effect is often absent. Dias, Pennycook and Rand showed Americans real headlines in Facebook format while varying whether the publisher was hidden, shown in grey text, or given a logo banner. In Study 1, with 562 participants, the interaction between source visibility and headline veracity was F = 1.59, p = .20 for accuracy judgements and F = 2.68, p = .068 for sharing intentions. Study 2 repeated the comparison with 1,845 participants to rule out low power and returned F = 0.02, p = .89 and F = 0.00, p = .97. Mang, Fennis and Epstude reviewed 91 misinformation studies covering 64,162 participants and coded 162 source-credibility effects: 77 were statistically significant, 65 were not, and 20 gave mixed evidence.

The partisan-cue strand replicates and varies. Tappin ran 34 contemporary American policy questions past 1,240 respondents, giving 7,460 observations, and estimated a mean treatment effect of party elite cues of 0.08, or 8% of the opinion scale. Tappin and Hewitt exposed US adults to party cues on five policy issues and polled them again three days later. Among the 773 respondents who completed both waves, the influence persisted at about 50% of its original magnitude.

study.cite: Kumkale, G. T., & Albarracín, D. (2004). The sleeper effect in persuasion: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 130(1), 143-172.

limits:
The founding study is one class. Sixty-one Yale men in a history course read four articles once, in 1951, and the sources included Pravda and a named physicist whose standing was particular to that decade. Two of the four topics carry political weight and two do not, and the paper reports no test of whether that mattered.

No effect size is quoted in the structured fields. Hovland and Weiss report net percentages of subjects changing opinion, the party-cue work reports movement in percent of an opinion scale, and Tappin's intervals are Bayesian. Converting any of them here would produce a figure that appears in no source. The d = 0.08 in the detail above measures longitudinal change in discounting-cue conditions, not the size of the source-credibility effect itself.

Three documents named here were not obtained. Cohen's 2003 'Party over policy', the paper most often cited for partisan source effects, is quoted only from its PubMed abstract, and no number from it appears on this page. Clemm von Hohenberg and Guess is paywalled at Cambridge Core; its title page and abstract were read and nothing else is quoted. Wilson and Sherrell's 1993 meta-analysis of source effects, which secondary literature treats as the quantitative summary of this area, was not obtained, and no figure from it is given. Bullock's range of 3% to 43% across party-cue studies is quoted here as Tappin describes it, not from Bullock's own paper.

Searches ran over Crossref by title and DOI, PubMed, the publisher pages at Oxford Academic, Cambridge Core, APA PsycNet and Springer, the Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review, and general web search. No meta-analysis of the immediate source-credibility effect on attitude change was read in full for this entry.
misreadings:
The sleeper effect is the part of Hovland and Weiss that survives in retellings, and it is the part that held up least well. Their crossing curves are real. Pooled over 72 data sets, the delayed rise after a discounting cue matches what happens to people given no message at all. The usual claim that a distrusted message gains force over time describes a pattern that is mostly the credible source losing force.

Source effects on persuasion and source effects on believing a news story are treated as one finding and behave differently. Emphasising the publisher of a real headline left accuracy judgements unmoved in a sample of 1,845, and across 91 misinformation studies fewer than half of the coded source effects reached significance.

Credibility did not change what Hovland and Weiss's readers took in. Their quiz scores were 3.36 against 3.26 immediately and 2.58 against 2.67 four weeks later. The distrusted source was read and remembered, and then discounted.

A source cue is not an authority instruction and not a hostile reading of coverage. Compliance with a command belongs to authority bias and partisan judgements of slant to the hostile media effect. Filing all three under one name imports evidence between three literatures that measure different things.

The party-cue result is often quoted as though one number covered it. Across 34 issues put to the same respondents, the mean effect was 8% of the opinion scale. The spread between issues was wide, and Tappin puts it at between a third and two thirds of the variation seen across the published literature.
